Equations across degenerate points

Exposition and figures by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Original exposition and exercises: CC0. Supplied programme prerequisites retain their stated licences.

A differential equation with a vanishing leading coefficient cannot always be solved by dividing that coefficient away. Such a division gives the ordinary solutions on the complementary intervals, but says nothing about which branches extend through the zero or which concentrated terms remain possible. We combine exact division, primitives and finite-order estimates to answer those questions.

Distributions act complex linearly. We use , , and . The following complete earlier proofs supply the operations:

  • Jumps, point jets and smooth division, Proposition 1 and Theorems 3 and 5, give finite jet products, division by coordinate powers, and the complete kernel of a smooth multiplier without flat zeros.
  • Primitives and endpoint extension, Theorem 1, gives primitives on intervals and proves that their whole ambiguity is a constant.
  • Weak equations and classical functions, Theorems 3.1 and 4.1, prove the integrating-factor and jump rules.
  • Finite parts of singular powers, Corollary 2.2, Lemma J, Theorem 4.1 and Proposition 5.1, give the one-sided finite parts, finite point-jet structure, their Euler identities and the principal value.

Reflection sends to the negative-side indicator with a minus sign when the coordinate is moved past reflection. Thus gives as distributions. The values of the indicators at zero are immaterial.

A coefficient multiplying the derivative alone

Theorem 6 (piecewise constants and the allowed point terms). Let be an open interval and have no flat zeros. Denote its zero set by , its multiplicity at by , and the connected components of by . All solutions of are An inner sum is empty at a simple zero. All coefficients are arbitrary. Both sums are locally finite on .

Proof: the ordinary part. The division lesson proves that is locally finite. On each component , multiplication by gives , so is a constant there. Only finitely many components meet a fixed compact subinterval of : their separating zeros lie in that interval, apart from its two boundary components. Thus is locally integrable. On a compact test, integrate by parts on its finitely many component pieces. The outer boundary terms vanish with the test, and the interior endpoints give where are the constants on the immediately adjacent intervals. Since , this implies .

Proof: the concentrated part. The difference is supported on . Near an isolated zero , the point-support theorem gives a finite sum . Independence therefore forces The remaining degrees are exactly those in (D21). Their sum over is a distribution because it is locally finite. Subtracting it from gives zero on every zero neighborhood and on ; local uniqueness makes the difference zero throughout .

Conversely, (D22) and the coordinate-power product formula show that every distribution in (D21) satisfies (D20). Each choice of component constants and jet coefficients is unique, by restriction to the components and then by independent tests near each zero.

Exercise 8 (advanced) — order zero and continuity. Prove that every solution of has distributional order at most zero. Determine those represented by continuous functions.

Solution. In (D24), the component function is locally bounded and only finitely many point masses meet any compact set. Its pairing is therefore bounded by a compact-dependent constant times the sup norm of the test. This proves order at most zero even when the coefficient sequences are unbounded.

If a continuous function represents the distribution, each point coefficient must vanish. After subtracting the bounded component function, a nonzero point coefficient would be represented near its isolated point by a locally integrable function. Tests with value one at that point, bounded by one and supported in shrinking intervals, have point-mass pairing equal to that nonzero coefficient but locally integrable pairing tending to zero by dominated convergence. This is impossible. The function is constant on each component, and continuity at every endpoint makes adjacent constants equal. Since the intervals form one chain, the function is one constant on the line. Conversely every constant solves the equation.
